messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Finn, a 26-year-old fisherman, had come to us seeking help for the persistent shadows cast by an experience of torture several years prior. He was a newly married man, but his wife was increasingly concerned by the changes in his behaviour, which had intensified since their wedding. The traumatic event had occurred when Finn, then a young deckhand, was captured while fishing in disputed international waters. He was held for months in a makeshift prison, subjected to repeated interrogations and physical abuse. He vividly remembered being confined for long periods in a small, dark cell, often forced into excruciatingly painful positions that left his body contorted, creating a searing agony in his limbs and back. During one particularly brutal session, he recalled the distant, faint cries of a baby, a sound that merged with his own terror and the muffled sounds of his captors. Another indelible memory was the disorienting, terrifying journey in the back of a windowless van, its engine rumbling and stopping like a public bus, as he was transported blindfolded and bound, utterly helpless and exposed. The systematic cruelty left him feeling profoundly vulnerable, a sensation that had never truly left him.

After his release, Finn struggled to reintegrate into his life and work. The world, which once felt predictable, now seemed fraught with hidden dangers. He found himself constantly on edge, his senses hyper-alert. Now, any time Finn encounters a trigger, the past rushes back with overwhelming force. Just last week, while on shore leave, he was riding a bus into town when the familiar rumble and jostle of the vehicle instantly dragged him back to that terrifying journey in captivity. As his mind was thrust into this memory of what happened, he felt his body tense, his muscles instinctively trying to brace against an unseen blow, his back aching with the phantom pain of being held in those torturous positions. He reported that when these memories return, he often feels intense rage, a burning anger at his captors and the injustice he suffered.

This visceral re-experiencing of the past immediately ignites a profound sense of threat in the present. The memory of his confinement and the pain it entailed makes him feel as if he is still in imminent danger, his heart pounding, his breath shallow. This pervasive feeling of being threatened has become a constant companion. At home, he meticulously listens for sounds that might mean someone is entering his house, often startling at the creak of floorboards or the rustle of leaves outside. When he and his wife go out, he finds himself meticulously scanning every room, unable to relax unless his back is against a wall, allowing him to see everyone and everything. He also has an uncanny ability to notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, from a discarded bottle on the street to a heavy wrench in the ship’s engine room.

What complicates matters further is the cyclical nature of his distress. This constant, exhausting vigilance and heightened sense of threat itself frequently pulls Finn back into fragmented memories of his torture. His mind, perpetually searching for danger, replays scenes from his captivity, trying to anticipate and prepare for future harm, inadvertently reinforcing the power of those traumatic memories. This relentless rumination on past dangers, fueled by his present fear, also makes him exquisitely sensitive to anything that might signal a recurrence. Because he feels so perpetually unsafe and vigilant, his brain has become hyper-attuned, turning once-innocuous stimuli like the rumble of a bus or the sound of a baby's cry into potent alarms, creating more triggers in his daily life. Even the feeling of emotional vulnerability, such as when he tries to discuss his struggles with his wife, can trigger the memory of his helplessness, leading him to withdraw further.

Finn’s occupation as a fisherman, which once provided a sense of purpose and freedom, now often places him in situations that exacerbate his symptoms. The enclosed spaces on the boat, the rhythmic sounds of the engines, and the vast, isolating stretches of the ocean can all stir his anxiety. His inability to relax, his constant scanning for threats, and his tendency to withdraw when feeling vulnerable have begun to strain his marriage, leading to arguments and a growing distance between him and his wife. He came to therapy because he recognizes that his life has become a constant battle against an invisible enemy, and he desperately wants to break free from the tightening grip of his past before it consumes his future.
